name: Wendy Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Wendy, thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no links to companies, unions or parties, and what you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior operator in the knitting room at Holm Textiles. We make stretchy technical fabric for car seats and for medical supports, like knee braces. I look after fourteen circular knitting machines, those big round ones that spin a tube of fabric, and I train the new starters. Most of my day is threading yarn, catching dropped stitches before they run, and changing needles.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm good at it, which helps. I can spot a needle about to break by the line it leaves in the fabric. And Holm is ten minutes from our flat, and the next textile job is in another region. The pay's low for what I do, but it's steady, and steady matters when you've got two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. So AI's a bit of a damp squib.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most new things, useful in places and oversold everywhere else. At work I'd say let's get on with it. I'm not one for arguing about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life stays the same, which is fine but not great. Me and Tom (my partner) are saving for a wedding and we've managed four hundred in a year. The car needs tyres and Tom's warehouse cut his hours in the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep training the new ones, because that's what gets me noticed. I'd ask about the shift supervisor role when Gloria retires next year, which pays about a hundred more a month. And I'd keep using the AI on my phone for the odd thing, like the wedding budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit stuck. Like waiting for a bus that's late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom's hours were cut. What happens if that happens again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the wedding fund becomes the tyre fund, like it did in August. We'd manage, but it'd be another year of not getting married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI for the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I just tell it what we earn and what we spend and ask where the money's going. I didn't need a robot to tell me we spend eighty a month on takeaways, but it was embarrassing in writing.

say: AI is **useful in places** and oversold everywhere else.
At work she'd say **get on with it**, not argue online.
think: Life stays the same, with **four hundred** saved for the wedding in a year.
Tom's warehouse **cut his hours** in summer, and the car needs tyres.
do: Keep **training new starters** to get noticed.
Ask about the **supervisor role** when Gloria retires.
Use the **AI app** for the wedding budget.
feel: **Fine** but **stuck**, like waiting for a late bus.
S0.quote: I didn't need a robot to tell me we spend eighty a month on takeaways, but it was embarrassing in writing.
fieldNote: She's **pragmatic** about AI: a budgeting helper, nothing more.
Household strain comes from Tom's **unsteady hours** and slow wedding savings.
She sees the **supervisor role** as her realistic next step.

steps.text: Apply for the knitting room supervisor role when Gloria retires
Cut takeaways to save toward the wedding
Track the household budget with the AI app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, office first, machines later. That sounds believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should all learn a bit about the new tools so nobody gets left behind. In the knitting room I'd say our hands are safe for now, but the planning and ordering upstairs will change. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my machines are safe for a good while, but Tom worries me more. His warehouse already has scanners telling him where to walk, and they're talking about robot trolleys. If my partner's warehouse job goes, we're on my wage alone, and my wage doesn't cover the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the course if Holm offered training on the new planning screens, once I saw someone else get on with it. I'd tell Tom to look for something with his hands that robots won't reach soon, maybe the forklift licence. And we'd push the wedding back a year to save harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More for Tom than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for someone else to try it first. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Nadia in quality, she's always first with a new phone. If Nadia says the planning screen is fine, I'll learn it the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pushing the wedding back. How does Tom feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes and then go quiet for a day. He's the romantic one. I'm the one with the spreadsheet.

Hands in the knitting room are safe **for now**; upstairs will change.
think: Her **machines** are safe for a good while.
Tom's **warehouse job** is at risk, and her wage alone doesn't cover rent.
do: Take Holm's **planning screen** training once a colleague proves it.
Urge Tom to get a **forklift licence**.
**Postpone the wedding** a year to save harder.
S1.quote: If my partner's warehouse job goes, we're on my wage alone, and my wage doesn't cover the rent.
fieldNote: Her worry shifts to her **partner's job**, which she sees as more exposed.
Classic **steady** adopter: she'll learn once a colleague like Nadia proves it.
The **wedding** is the first thing she trades away.

steps.text: Take the planning screen training after Nadia tries it
Help Tom book a forklift licence course
Move the wedding back a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our wedding, even on the old plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to do something serious and quick, because nobody's ready. I'm not political, but I'd want a straight answer from whoever's in charge about what happens to people like us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the office at Holm is gone by 2028 and the knitting room by 2031. Knitting machines are already half robots. They just need someone to thread them and fix them. Tom's warehouse would go even faster. We'd both be out in a few years with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking right away at jobs where you deal with people, maybe a care assistant, because Tom's mum does that. I'd move any savings into paying off the car. And I'd use the AI more, to write job applications and learn what's out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, like the floor's tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work. Is that something you'd want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Want, no. I like machines more than people, if I'm honest. But I'd rather have a job I don't love than no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in the three years before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those are the years I'd be learning something new while still working at Holm. Nights and weekends. And Tom and I would probably move in with his mum to save rent.

say: The government must do something **serious and quick**.
She'd want a **straight answer** about what happens to people like her.
think: Holm's office goes by **2028** and the knitting room by 2031.
Both she and Tom could be **out of work** with nothing saved.
do: Look into **care assistant** jobs straight away.
Use savings to **pay off the car**.
feel: **Properly scared**, like the floor is tilting.
S2.quote: Knitting machines are already half robots. They just need someone to thread them and fix them.
fieldNote: She sees knitting machines as **already half automated**, which sharpens her fear.
She'd choose **any steady job** over none, even care work she doesn't want.
Both incomes at risk pushes her toward **family support**.

steps.text: Apply for care assistant training through Tom's mum's home
Pay off the car loan with savings
Move in with Tom's mum to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Long enough to plan, short enough to sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get organised, not panic. At work I'd say let's ask Holm what the plan is, now, while there's time to train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me room to get one more skill. The thinking AI in 2031 hits Holm's office first, and the knitting room has until 2034. That's seven years for me. Enough to get a certificate, not enough to waste time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into the industrial maintenance certificate at the college, the one that runs on Saturdays. I'd save fifty a month by cutting takeaways, which the AI already caught us on. And we'd get married on a small budget instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but steady. Like before a driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get married sooner here. Why the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the knitting room goes in 2034, I'd rather be married and settled first. A small do at the community hall, forty people, done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the course didn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have Holm until the robots come. I'd go back to looking at care work. I like having a plan B.

say: Now is the time to **get organised**, not panic.
Ask Holm for its **plan** while there's time to train people.
think: Five years gives her room for **one more skill**.
With the knitting room safe until **2034**, she has seven years.
do: Join the Saturday **industrial maintenance** course at the college.
Save **fifty a month** by cutting takeaways.
Get married on a **small budget** instead of waiting.
feel: **Worried but steady**, like before a driving test.
S3.quote: If the knitting room goes in 2034, I'd rather be married and settled first.
fieldNote: She does the **arithmetic** on her own timeline: seven years for hands-on work.
Unlike the slow scenario, she now wants the **wedding sooner**.
She keeps **care work** as a plan B.

steps.text: Enrol in the Saturday industrial maintenance course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort things out sensibly, so let's not lose our heads. I'd say the company and the college should work together on courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly okay. I'd get the supervisor job, save a bit, get married, and then in a few years train for something with more future. Tom would have time to change too. The in-between money is what I'd worry about, not 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the supervisor role at Holm. I'd keep using the AI for little things and learn a bit more as it gets better. And I'd put twenty a month aside for a course in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Like a dentist appointment months away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tom would have time too. What would he do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the forklift licence and then something in maintenance, like me. We joke we'll open a repair shop one day. Probably just a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the area?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in five years, if Holm looked shaky. But my mum's here and Tom's mum is here. We'd stay as long as we could.

Holm and the college should **work together** on courses.

Her worry is the **in-between money**, not 2039.
do: Go for the **supervisor role** at Holm.
Save **twenty a month** for a future course.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like a dentist appointment months away.
S4.quote: The in-between money is what I'd worry about, not 2039.
fieldNote: The long warning lets her follow the **normal path** first, then retrain.
Ties to **both mothers** keep her in the area.

steps.text: Apply for the knitting room supervisor role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd take Tom's job and mine in a few years and we've got nothing saved. What would help is short courses that are free and on weekends, so you can keep earning while you learn. And someone telling us honestly which jobs will still be there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about couples. Everyone talks about one person's job. But when two people on low wages both work with their hands, it's the whole house that goes.

headlineQuote: When two people on low wages both work with their hands, it's the whole house that goes.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** senior knitting operator at Holm Textiles, making car seat and medical fabric.
She lives with her partner Tom, a **warehouse worker**, and they're saving slowly for a wedding.
**Pragmatic** and centrist, she uses AI now and then and learns new tools once proven.
Her main fear is **both incomes** failing together, especially in the fast scenarios.
With more warning she plans a **maintenance certificate** and keeps care work as plan B.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would take both her job and Tom's with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Free weekend courses** so people can earn while learning.
Honest information about **which jobs** will last.
